answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: These are the closing lines of “Little Gidding,” the fourth and final poem in Eliot’s Four Quartets — first published as a standalone poem in 1942 and collected with the other three quartets in 1943. The wording is confirmed against the published text of the poem.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: September/October 1942 (pamphlet & New English Weekly); collected in Four Quartets, 1943

source.excerpt:
We shall not cease from exploration
And the end of all our exploring
Will be to arrive where we started
And know the place for the first time.
trail: Eliot finished “Little Gidding” by 19 September 1942, and it first appeared that October in the New English Weekly, per the Wikipedia entry on the poem ↗. Faber & Faber then issued it as a separate first-edition pamphlet (Gallup A42) on 1 December 1942, per first-edition bibliographic listings ↗.
All four quartets were then collected as Four Quartets, published in New York in 1943 and London in 1944, confirmed by the Wikipedia entry on Four Quartets ↗.
The exact wording of the closing lines is confirmed by a quotation reference page quoting the poem directly: Goodreads quote page citing Little Gidding, Four Quartets ↗.
source.excerptNote: The final stanza of “Little Gidding.” The popular quotation compresses the first two lines into one sentence.

source.rightsNote: “Little Gidding” was first published in 1942 and collected in Four Quartets in 1943 — well after the 1930 public-domain cutoff for the United States — so the poem remains under copyright, administered by Faber & Faber on behalf of the Eliot Estate.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: This is the closing stanza of “Little Gidding,” the fourth of Eliot’s Four Quartets, meditating on time, memory, and spiritual return — the idea that a journey outward ends in a renewed, deeper recognition of where one began.

Eliot wrote the poem during the Second World War while serving as an air-raid warden in London; “Little Gidding” takes its title from the Anglican religious community in Huntingdonshire that Eliot visited in 1936.
context.pull: And the end of all our exploring will be to arrive where we started and know the place for the first time.
